_what: What computer/shell-string-scan.mjs refuses in the code that runs on a person's Mac and in the Worker: running a program by building ONE command string a shell reads (page-, model- or person-supplied words can then become commands). A helper is called with an argument array (execFile, spawn without a shell, Swift Process.arguments), so each word stays one word. `roots` are the folders scanned (relative to the repository), `skip_folders` are never read, `extensions` are the files read. Each rule has a `files` list (the extensions it applies to), a `pattern` (a JavaScript regular expression source, flags `m`), an optional `only_when_file_matches` (the rule applies only to a file whose text matches it, so the name `exec` of a database handle is not confused with child_process.exec), and the `say` shown for a hit. `allowed` names a file and the reason a hit there is safe; a row with no reason is refused by the test. Adding a rule or an exception is a row here, flipped without compiling.

rules.say: child_process exec/execSync hands one string to a shell; call the program with execFile and an argument array.
child_process exec/execSync hands one string to a shell; call the program with execFile and an argument array.
A spawn or execFile with shell set runs its arguments through a shell; leave shell off and pass an argument array.
A shell -c command built from variables lets those words become commands; pass them to the program as separate arguments.

allowed.because: the command is typed by the person on this receiver's own command line (--work, --wake, --on); the job and event words reach it on standard input, never in the command string
the only word placed in the string is a commit id read from git rev-parse of origin/main, and the folder is the script's own build folder; this release script belongs to the release owner
